Our interests include programming, scientific research, data analysis, and technological innovation. We bring strengths in analytical thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and collaboration, with interests in Python, Java, software development, and advanced technology. We are driven by curiosity and scientific discovery.
summary:
When rivers and lakes flood into forests, the water spreads under the trees, where cameras can't see it even on a clear day. Clouds and darkness hide it too. The L-band radar on NASA-ISRO's NISAR satellite sees through all three: water beneath tree trunks bounces the radar signal back brightly. DELTA PULSE makes that radar usable by anyone.

Type any place on Earth. DELTA PULSE searches NASA's ASF archive live and reads only the parts of the real NISAR GCOV files it needs, with no 1.9 GB downloads. Within seconds it shows what changed: radar maps, a time series of every pass, rainfall and cloud context, and same-day NASA camera images that reveal what the clouds hid. "Your Story" turns any place into a narrated, animated documentary about its hidden water.

Every statement is labelled OBSERVED, CALCULATED, INTERPRETED or UNCONFIRMED, so the app never claims a flood it can't prove. In our Tonle Sap (Cambodia) case study, the radar signature of water under vegetation grew about 6.6×, from 260 to 1,704 km², while clouds covered more than half the sky at 9 of 10 pass times. Independent checks support this: the water class finds 82% of Landsat's permanent water, and the flooded area tracks river flow (r = 0.81).
details:
THE PROBLEM

When a river or lake floods into a forest, the water spreads beneath the trees. Optical satellites can't see it, even on a clear day, and in flood season the sky is rarely clear. At Tonle Sap in Cambodia, clouds covered more than half the sky at 9 of the 10 satellite pass times we studied. Yet this hidden water matters: seasonal flood pulses drive fisheries, farming, drinking water and wetland health for millions of people.

The NASA-ISRO NISAR satellite can see it. Its 24 cm L-band radar passes through cloud, darkness and forest canopy. Open water reflects the signal away and looks dark. Water standing under trees bounces the signal off the water and then the trunks, straight back to the satellite, and looks bright. But NISAR data comes as 1.9 GB scientific files that need specialist software and training. DELTA PULSE removes that barrier.

WHAT IT DOES

DELTA PULSE is a web app where anyone can type a place on Earth and see how its surface water changed, using real NISAR radar.

- Explore: search any place. The app finds every NISAR pass over it in NASA's ASF DAAC archive and, in about 10-15 seconds, shows radar maps, a time series of every pass, a "Radar Change Fingerprint", and rainfall, cloud and river-flow context.

- Camera vs radar: NASA GIBS camera images (MODIS, VIIRS) of the same day sit beside the radar, so you can see what the clouds hid.

- Your Story: turns any place into a narrated, animated documentary. It shows cloud cover at the exact hour the satellite passed, a radar flipbook, a hidden-water timeline, the moment of biggest change, and a chapter on what is and isn't known.

- Live globe: a 3D globe of NISAR's newest acquisitions, clickable to explore.

- Radar Lab and Scatter Lab: interactive models that teach how radar scattering works. In Scatter Lab you drag thresholds on real pixels and the map updates live.

- Hear the water: data sonification plays one note per pass, and rain sounds follow the real rainfall record.

- Practical features: 26 languages, share links, CSV and JSON downloads, an in-app user guide, phone support and reduced-motion support.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Discovery. The Python backend queries the ASF Search API for NISAR Level-2 GCOV products (provisional, validated and urgent-response collections) over the chosen place.

2. Remote reading. Instead of downloading whole files, the backend reads each file's HDF5 chunk index and fetches only the chunks covering the area of interest, using parallel HTTP range requests. A 20 km window of a 1.9 GB file arrives in seconds.

3. Quality control. NASA's own quality masks are applied. We verified two different file layouts on real data. Product releases are never mixed, and area figures count only ground seen on every pass.

4. Screening. HH and HV backscatter (gamma-naught) are sorted into two classes: water-like ground (low backscatter) and a double-bounce signature consistent with water under vegetation (bright HH, large HH minus HV).

5. Context. The app adds ERA5 rainfall and cloud cover, GloFAS river discharge, and same-day NASA GIBS imagery, always kept visually distinct from the NISAR measurements.

6. Presentation. A Next.js frontend draws the maps, charts, story and globe.

WHAT WE FOUND

Case study: Tonle Sap Lake, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lake and a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve, over 10 NISAR passes from 19 June to 17 October 2026.

- The radar signature of water under vegetation grew about 6.6 times, from 260 to 1,704 km², peaking on 11 September.

- Water-like ground grew 48%, from 1,829 to 2,703 km².

- The growth was concentrated within 20 km of the lake, as a real flood pulse would be.

HOW WE KNOW IT'S VALID

We checked the results against data that played no part in building the method.

- JRC Global Surface Water (Landsat, 1984-2021): our water class finds a median 82% of permanent water and flags at most 0.1% of never-wet land.

- GloFAS river flow: the radar's flooded area tracks flow in the Tonle Sap River (r = 0.81 over 10 dates). We label this honestly as a small sample with shared seasonality.

- ERA5 wind: light at every pass (0.5-4.2 m/s), so wind doesn't explain the changes.

- Sensitivity: the direction of change and the peak date hold when the water threshold moves by plus or minus 2 dB.

- Automated tests plus live end-to-end runs at Tonle Sap, Manaus, the Sundarbans, Jakarta, Dhaka and the Aleutians.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- Wetland and fisheries managers can track the flood pulse that fish breeding depends on.

- Water agencies and farmers can follow seasonal water through the cloudy months when cameras fail.

- Recovery planners can see where water stood after a flood.

- Students and the public can type their own home town and watch its story, with no training.

NISAR images nearly all land every 12 days, so DELTA PULSE works worldwide and suits seasonal and long-term monitoring more than hour-by-hour emergencies.

HOW IT'S CREATIVE

- It reads huge NISAR files remotely in seconds, which makes live worldwide search possible without big servers or storage.

- It writes a data documentary automatically for any place, with narration and sound.

- It treats honesty as a design feature: every statement is labelled OBSERVED, CALCULATED, INTERPRETED or UNCONFIRMED.

- It turns radar physics into things you can play with and hear.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty over hype. Bright double-bounce can also come from buildings, and wind can roughen water so it no longer looks dark. The classes are screening results, not calibrated flood maps, and the app says so.

- Fair comparison. We never mix product releases, and we compare only ground seen on every pass.

- Traceability. Every image shows its acquisition date, track, frame, release and when the archive was checked.

- Accessibility. Plain language, 26 languages, phone layouts, reduced motion, and a guide inside the app.

- Limits. NISAR's 12-day revisit, a documented data gap (27 July to 10 August 2026), and uneven coverage on some tracks.

TOOLS

Frontend: TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, proj4js, deployed on Vercel.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, asf_search, h5py, NumPy, pandas, pyproj, Shapely, Pillow, pytest.

Data: NISAR L2 GCOV (NASA ASF DAAC), NASA GIBS, ERA5 and GloFAS via Open-Meteo, JRC Global Surface Water, AWS Terrain Tiles, OpenStreetMap Nominatim.

An AI coding assistant (Anthropic Claude) helped write and debug code, directed and reviewed by the team.

NEXT STEPS

Calibration against river gauges, alerts for watched places (a scheduler already re-checks every 6 hours), and land-cover data to separate buildings from flooded forest.
